review_text_raw:
Okay, while I said I liked this game, [b]I think in terms of recommendation, this is more a "maybe" than an outright "yes."[/b] There are several things to consider before you purchase this one, and while I ultimately think you'll enjoy the experience either way, you may be slightly frustrated by at least one or two of these points. I know I was. 

(-) First, the game is short. It took me less than 4 hours to finish it, and that's with several long cut scenes. Speaking of those cut scenes... pay attention to them. I didn't, because some of them seemed pointless, and that led me to the only time I felt truly stuck in this game LOL.

(+) You play as an operator in the FDI, and the entire gameplay involves sitting in front of your computer, connecting dots, and solving puzzles. I absolutely loved it. It was fresh and interesting, and the feeling of things connecting and unraveling was really fun. I actually wish we had more of it—I would've gladly played more hours of more cases, slowly connecting them to this huge conspiracy. It made me hope that someone would make an entire mystery murder game (as opposed to a conspiracy) as "the guy in the chair," slowly unraveling everything and helping the "heroes" solve the mystery. 

(-/+) For a game that's sitting in front of your computer... the stakes are high and so is the tension. I actually got really anxious at parts, in a way that doesn't really happen with most games because, the way everything is set up, WE are Tenner. So I felt like there was a gun aimed at [i]me[/i] at times, LOL. For me, this was a point in favor of the game, but if you're looking for a more relaxed experience, this may not be it. 

(-/+) The ending. Personally? Not a fan. Oh, I loved the reveal. The minute [i]I[/i] started connecting the dots, my stomach dropped. 10/10 for that. But everything after that?... I will be playing the next game, if there is one, but overall, [spoiler]I am not really the kind of person to enjoy an "everybody died" ending. After all the brilliant puzzle solving, I wanted these characters to have a good ending. I have seen people talk about how this was actually a good ending - how Hal is still thwarting the organization 30 years later, and that's realistic and optimistic but damn. I got attached to [i]these[/i] characters. I wanted to see them happy, even if we fail to totally crush the bad guys in the end of the game. And I wanted to understand what the goal of the "bad guys" in this game is, and I don't. They're evil people, but... why are they doing what they're doing? No clue. Which is another thing I don't like. For me, a game needs to be able to stand on its own, even if it's part of a larger narrative. [/spoiler] Essentially, this felt like a game meant to [i]set up[/i] another game, and truthfully, I don't like that.

review_text_raw:
Hello developers,

I just finished playing your game on the Switch, and I immediately bought the Steam version to add to my library. The game's atmosphere and narrative pacing really drew me in, and the background music was perfectly fitting. Because of this, I'm happy to leave a positive review, though it also left me with higher expectations.

 [spoiler]
The game is about four hours long, and playing it felt more like watching a movie. However, as a game, it offered too few choices for the player. During my play through, I tried to deliberately not answer the supervisor's calls or even pretended to be a 'good kid' to see if there was a way to betray HAL. But the game didn't give me any more options. I believe that in an interactive story game, player choices and their consequences are its true charm and what keeps players engaged.
The bomb disposal segment really stood out. I felt a strong sense of immersion and genuinely enjoyed being able to help someone. It's a shame that, probably due to the game's length, such a brilliant sequence only happened once.
The core puzzle was very cleverly designed, and its reveal was absolutely an adrenaline rush. I completely understand what you, as developers, wanted players to feel with that ending—the horror, the profound sense of melancholy, the sadness for the characters, and the lingering regret that a bigger enemy wasn't truly dealt with. However, even after experiencing all that, I still wished players could help the characters achieve a good ending. I truly love these characters.
Overall, this is a fantastic game! I really hope to play more from you in the future!
[/spoiler]

I hardly ever write reviews for games... However, after this one...
Just play it. 
You won't regret it. 

I went in thinking it was going to be a basic puzzle solving operator simulator game...HOW WRONG I WAS. 
This game, I should've seen it coming. I should've seen where it was going...But it kept me too immersed to really care about anything else. This is such a beautifully written concept turned into an equally beautiful game. 

Games never leave an impression on me, really. I mean I play them, I have my favorites. But this is the first game that has EVER given me chills, shocked me to my core, and my stomach dropped more times than I care to admit. This was a beautiful game. Absolutely fabulously, wonderfully, beautifully, amazingly well crafted game and I look forward to any other game this company produces. 

Thank you, Devs, for this beautiful masterpiece.

review_text_raw:
--- BUY THIS GAME WHEN IT IS ON SALE ---

I paid ~ $13.00 and that is TOO much for this game. I think a fair price for this game is $5.00 due to play hours and lack of replayability.

PROs:

+ I like investigative puzzle games and this one was intriguing.
+ Story was compelling.
+ I liked the idea of using different systems to discover information and link said information together.
+ I am looking forward to a sequel. Hopefully it will be longer than this game.

CONs:

- I beat it twice in 7 hours so average game play time was 3.5 hours. I really only played it twice to get the achievements though.
     - I don't think the price of the game should be this high for such a short game. Especially since there isn't a lot of replayability with this game :/.
- The story gives the illusion of choice but regardless of dialogue options, you still end up where you are intended to go; very RAILROADY
- The game has investigative tools but for most of them you only use them once throughout the entire game.
- For my second playthrough, I was REALLY wanting a skip button for scenes where the protagonist "goes home at the end of the day;" It was really boring to sit through those scenes.
- There are some locked files that you don't get access to, which was disappointing. There were many missed opportunities to build lore or give players opportunities to poke around, even if they resulted in dead ends, it would have been nice to fill out the world a little more.
- It would have been nice if there was a reward/punishment system for being smart or needing to have your hand held through the whole game. Some sort of variable input that would impact the game based on player actions. Like a trust meter so if people trust you, it is easier to lie to them or something.

I know it sounds like I am taking a huge dump on this game but my goal is to help the developers with the sequel.The game has A LOT of good ideas, I just think the execution and the offering could have been better.

That being said, I liked the game and I want to see more from this developer.

review_text_raw:
Conspiratorial thinking is kinda like anime girls. Like, okay. So there's this super hot princess from planet catgirl who's on the run from the space mafia, and she just so happens to teleport naked right into your bathtub. While you're in it. And because of this, she's super into you for some reason. Yeah, sounds nice, but this is so insanely removed from how actual relationships form, it's like watching aliens mate (I mean... she is an alien, so...)

And with conspiracies it's like: okay, so there's this ultra-powerful cabal of politicians, billionaires and celebrities, who completely control the society without being spotted... but then they reveal themselves by using symbols in plain sight. And the person to stop them? A bumbling born-into-wealth TV-star who in fact is a 5D-chess player, so all his obvious mistakes are actually genius moves that you just don't get. I don't know guys, seems very legit, but there are a few pieces of this story that make me question its validity.

Think about how a real conspiracy of this scale would work. Incomprehensible wealth would be poured into world-class assassins and operatives to ensure compliance or silence. Evidence would be erased with brutal efficiency, with red herrings and multiple layers of scapegoats; but even then, people are people, and eventually something could possibly slip the cracks. 

The Operator explores this more realistic portrayal of conspiracies, with the scale also being somewhat more realistic. You don't know who you can trust and who you can't. But not everyone (except you) is in on it.

Right?

But hold on. Before you start yelling LOOMINARTY CONFIRMED and smoking dat 420 MLG style, some actual work needs to be done. You're an [strike]FBI[/strike] FDI operator with an access to a pretty sweet database, but also a job to do - to support agents in the field. Whatever confirming of loominarty you'll be doing will have to be squeezed in between protecting and serving those who [strike]are supposed to[/strike] protect and serve. Or perhaps these things could be related?

Wouldn't that be convenient.

Even with all your state-of-the-art tech you'll still have to think outside the box here. And pay attention. You might not find the all-seeing eye, but a funny detail here, a reappearing pattern there, and you just might find something that you're not supposed to.

But it's a dangerous game. For you, and for whoever [i]they[/i] might see as your ally. Things might get tense. Your palms will sweat, your heart will go a little bit faster. Someone's life might be on the line. And you're the only one that picked up the phone.

Still: this little journey might have what you could call flaws. I won't tell you what they are, because I think they don't really alter the value of the experience. You're a clever person; I'm sure you can see what I mean.

(if you're not that clever, you might want to skip this one, I've seen some really funny comments on the forums from people getting stuck because they missed some stuff)

And if my words alone don't convince you, you might want to know that the (achievement-sourced) percentage of people who have beaten the game is 67%. The only game with a number higher than this is Linelith, but that's a puzzle game that can be beaten in an hour. Draw your own conclusions.

7/10 Mixed feelings but recommend.

Mostly I just wish the game was longer- it takes 2-3 hours to complete this across four in game days. We hit our first major plot beat on day 1 and every case is tightly related. Our only break is the cutscene of downtime between shifts (which honestly, great touch, love it). I would have preferred a longer game with a slower burn. A longer gameplay time could have also given us the chance to master these systems and use that mastery later, but no such luck.

Plot wise the twists felt obvious just because its such a tightly focused story, but they really stuck the ending so I'm overall positive on it.

Some straightforward plug A into B puzzles, but a couple of quite novel ones that were fun to see play out.

Price seems like a reasonable ask, and for what appears to be a first game this shows a lot of promise- I'd love to see what the Operator 2 looks like (though personally I hope it is an unrelated, standalone tale, just for the sake of that slower burn).

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 98:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆☆ (8/10)

[i] The Operator [/i] casts you not as a hero in the field, but as the analyst—the voice behind the computer—supporting agents from the shadows. It’s a fascinating setup and a fresh twist on crime-solving games, and usually almost always lives up to its potential!

🖥[b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*] Authentic "operator" fantasy. You monitor missions from your desk, field phone calls, look through mysterious documents, and scrub through CCTV footage. 

[*] Diverse tools. The game gives you a chem scanner, facial recognition database, image enhancement tech, and document search systems. For example, in one mission, you identify a suspect by cross-referencing a blurry security camera with an equally blurry security footage of his car and license plate. That kind of detective work feels cool. You feel smart when it works.

[*] Great use of puzzles under pressure. A standout moment has you guiding a field agent through bomb defusal. You have to analyze chemicals, check your reference files, and read out step-by-step instructions—all while the timer ticks down. These time-sensitive missions are where the game shines.

[*] Well-done audio design. The UI clicks, radio static, and phone calls all contribute to a grounded, late-'90s thriller vibe. The voice acting is low-key but sells the scenario well, especially during moments of stress or confusion.

[*] No filler. It’s tight and focused. No wandering, no padding. You’re thrown into the action quickly and missions move at a brisk pace.
[/list]

[b]🧾 Cons: [/b]
[list]
[*] Flat characters. The field agents and mysterious hacker HAL are more archetypes than flesh-and-blood. They push the story forward, but rarely surprise

[*] Choices don’t matter much. There are dialogue branches, but most are cosmetic. Whether you’re professional or snarky, or even whether you succeed or fail at certain puzzles, the game mostly funnels you into the same story beats.

[*] Abrupt ending. The game ends just as things get interesting. HAL’s storyline ramps up, then vanishes. You barely get to dig into the conspiracy or see the consequences of your actions. It feels like a miniseries that ends on episode three.
[/list]

review_text_raw:
Aesthetically pleasing, good story with at the very least, decent voice acting if not great. Runs well. An interesting gameplay mechanic that has you sitting at your desk, putting together pieces of the puzzles as agents sweep the field for evidence and follow the leads you help develop. The story has you unraveling a conspiracy, using computer tools, metadata, and analyzing software to pull the narrative together. It's fascinating, and the game does a really good job at making you feel like you're truly a professional analyst, solving crimes from the comfort of a desk in Washington DC.

Problem is, the game is pretty darn short. Only about 4 hours of gameplay, and it feels deeply on rails, to the point that the puzzle portion of it feels more like a addon to the rest of the game. If you subscribe to the $1 per hour mindset, even discounted to $9, this game is technically not worth it, as the game has limited replayability. Though, the game does make up for it with the story and gameplay to a degree. It is, at the very least, a pretty impactful 4 hours, and you could get somewhat different results if you repeat the story, so there is a small sense that your choices matter. 

I might just be spoiled, coming off of The Roottrees are Dead which had a fairly similar premise of using a computer to uncover information that can fill in the blanks. But in TRaD, they introduce you to the tools and then you spend a bulk of the time using them on your own to fill in profiles on the family tree. There was a lot more blanks to fill in and time to spend fiddling around with information. With TO, you get introduced to cool mechanics and tools on your computer, and then use almost none of them ever again. The game feels like a 4 hour tutorial other than the story, which takes interesting turns and, as a flipside, keeps the player continously faced with new and interesting problems to solve. It sucks not being able to repeatedly use a mechanic I got familiar with or a handbook I just learned, but every in-game day pulls me straight in with a curveball, gameplay wise or story wise.

The ending kinda left a bad taste in my mouth. AFAIK, your choices don't really seem to affect the ending from what I saw online in guides and gameplay.

Still gonna leave it as a positive review, because I quite enjoyed this and I think the devs are absolutely cooking here. I just hope the developers consider putting more meat on the bones of TO2, because it feels like there is a ton of potential for a truly great puzzle/detective game here that only gets partially realized.

review_text_raw:
This game is top notch. As an old school adventure fan this felt like a true Rise of the Dragon, Jeff Tunnell style game which has been sorely lacking in the current market. What I mean by that specifically is that the post-Life is Strange adventure genre has had a long period of hammy, melodramatic social messaging meant to impress small cliques of games journalists for accolades in their astroturfed outlets. The REAL culprit was ABUSE! Or HOMOPHOBIA! Or RACISM! And the game was a METAPHOR! This plot device was not terribly interesting to begin with but due to the applause and funding that comes to such projects, it left us with a decade of such tripe as developers scratched and clawed to be next in line at the Attaboy Club, with each new offering being more hamfisted and alarmist than the last (check my review of 'Jessika' for a hilarious instance of this).

The Operator, however, is just a good old fashioned hard boiled story about cover ups and corruption.  It has a couple of flaws, the primary one being the blurred out bokeh filters meant to act as cutscenes. There is a sorta-kinda in-story explanation for this, and a reason for it to justify a later puzzle, but really it just comes across as a way to avoid paying for cutscenes and as a way to bridge days together, which is understandable enough for a small team with not a lot of money. In future, I'd recommend bridging the days with some kind of interactive option at the character's apartment or neighborhood, or by just using comic book style art for the cutscenes. In any case that complaint is a nothing burger, the game is well worth it and I look forward to more!

Firstly, I'd like to preface my review, by saying if you are interested in this game. Do not watch a play through of it, try the demo, see if your engaged and then buy the game. This review is spoiler free.

A lovely crafted indie detective thriller, with a fantastic narrative story provided me with a very enjoyable and gripping 3/4 hours of game play on my first play through. The game has been painstakingly crafted down to every individual element, and it really shows, but this love creates a gripping, edge of your seat experience which will make you truly engage with every character and feel every emotion in a short space of time. The time setting is fantastic, blending a feel of early 2000 technology, with modern software and interface feel. When the game says use headphones, I usually disagree. But this is one of the rare examples which playing with headphones or a decent speaker set-up takes this from a game to a true experience.

The game has got an excellent blend of mixed media, cinematic and a truly atmospheric score that intertwines with the narrative in a beautiful way to create this experience. Throughout the game it makes you constantly think, am I making the right choices, is this how I solve this puzzle, and gives you everything you need to figure these out in a well executed manner without holding your hand too much. Even the achievements have been carefully thought out to provide you just enough information that your inquisitive brain wants to fully unravel and unlock each one.

Do I wish the game was longer? Yes. Am I disappointing by this? No, I loved every second of my playtime and strongly look forward to what the developer and his talented contributors bring next. Would I consider buying a future DLC expansion? Easily, this has been the most engaged with a game I've been for a very long time, and I would love to see what the developer brings to the operative universe next. 

This game is truly, one of those rare indie gems, that brings the passion and story into an over saturated gaming market, and really makes you wish more development companies (Especially AAA) had the same mentality and craft.

review_text_raw:
The Operator, developed by Bureau 81 and published by Bureau 81 together with indienova, is a tightly focused narrative puzzle game that transforms the quiet, procedural work of intelligence analysis into a tense and engaging thriller. Rather than placing players in the role of an action hero or field agent, the game casts them as a desk-bound operator, someone whose power comes not from physical presence but from information, observation, and deduction. This shift in perspective defines the entire experience, creating a game that feels intimate, cerebral, and deliberately restrained.

You play as Evan Tanner, a newly recruited operator working for the fictional Federal Department of Intelligence. Your job is to support agents in the field by analysing data, processing evidence, and drawing connections that others might miss. The game unfolds almost entirely through Evan’s workstation, presented as a simulated computer desktop filled with databases, analysis tools, messaging systems, and case files. This interface-driven approach immediately sets the tone: instead of cinematic spectacle, The Operator relies on immersion through routine, making the player feel like they are genuinely sitting at a government terminal late at night, piecing together fragments of truth.

Gameplay revolves around solving a series of cases that gradually escalate in complexity and importance. Early tasks feel procedural—identifying suspects, tracing movements, or cross-referencing records—but as the story unfolds, patterns begin to emerge and the stakes rise. Players are required to closely read documents, examine photos and videos, search databases, and interpret subtle clues hidden in plain sight. The puzzles reward attentiveness and logical reasoning, often asking players to synthesize information from multiple sources rather than relying on a single obvious answer. When a breakthrough occurs, it feels earned, the result of careful thought rather than trial and error.

As the narrative progresses, the game shifts from isolated casework into a broader conspiracy. A mysterious hacker begins to interfere with FDI systems, raising questions about surveillance, authority, and the reliability of the information you’re working with. This transition adds narrative tension without abandoning the game’s grounded tone. The story remains largely linear, but it is effectively paced, allowing suspense to build gradually as seemingly unrelated assignments reveal deeper connections. Dialogue and character interactions are understated, delivered through calls, messages, and system prompts rather than dramatic cutscenes, which reinforces the feeling that you are always working behind the scenes.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is how convincingly it uses its interface as both a storytelling and gameplay tool. Every window, search bar, and analysis program feels purposeful, and learning how to use these tools becomes part of the experience. While some mechanics are simplified or exaggerated for gameplay purposes, they remain believable within the fiction, maintaining immersion. The design encourages players to slow down, double-check assumptions, and think critically—mistakes often stem from overlooking details rather than misunderstanding mechanics.

Visually, The Operator embraces a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic inspired by older operating systems and institutional software. The interface is dense but readable, intentionally lacking visual flair in favor of authenticity. This design choice may feel dry to some players, but it suits the game’s themes perfectly, emphasizing bureaucracy, control, and the monotony of surveillance work. Subtle audio cues, ambient hums, and restrained music enhance tension without distracting from concentration, allowing the player’s focus to remain on the task at hand.

In terms of pacing, the game strikes a careful balance. It is compact, typically completed in a handful of hours, but it avoids feeling rushed. Each case builds naturally on the last, and the increasing narrative weight keeps momentum strong. The linear structure limits replayability, as choices rarely branch into significantly different outcomes, but this also allows the developers to maintain tight narrative control and deliver a coherent, focused story without filler.

Community reception reflects appreciation for the game’s originality and execution. Players who enjoy detective work, mystery narratives, and “games on a computer” style experiences frequently praise its atmosphere and puzzle design. Criticism tends to focus on its short length, limited player agency, and occasional moments where immersion is broken by game-like constraints. Even so, these issues rarely overshadow the strengths of the experience, particularly for players aligned with its intended audience.

Taken as a whole, The Operator is a confident and distinctive narrative puzzle game that finds tension in observation rather than action. It succeeds by committing fully to its premise, turning data analysis and desk work into compelling gameplay through thoughtful design and strong thematic focus. While it may not appeal to players seeking open-ended systems or high replay value, it offers a memorable, tightly constructed experience for those who enjoy slow-burn storytelling, logical deduction, and the quiet unease of uncovering truths from behind a screen.

Rating: 9/10

Fantastic game, very enjoyable. You play as a call-operator for the "FDI", helping field agents to analyse the evidence they're obtaining. It's like you're at a screen with a headset, using the information to help solve crimes, and eventually, to get to the heart of the growing conspiracy that you begin to suspect within the FDI itself...

Very intuitive to play, with the right level of puzzles that don't bog you down, and a brilliant story and voice-acting to help make it as immersive as possible. If you want to pretend to work at the FBI, this is a good game for you :) Also, passing or failing at various key points seems to lead to multiple endings, leading to a certain amount of replayability.

STEAM DECK COMPATIBILITY: This game functions perfectly well on the steam deck, but I highly recommend playing this game at a desk PC with over-ear headphones on; the game has been designed to be immersive and this setup helps that the most.
